analysis.one_liner: Opens the Superior National Forest watershed to copper mining by lifting a federal ban and forcing canceled leases to be reissued.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 212-203 on April 30, 2024, but the Senate never took it up, so the federal mining ban near the Boundary Waters stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill wipes out a federal order that withdrew about 225,000 acres of federal land next to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness from new mineral leasing, and it orders the government to hand back mineral leases that were canceled in 2022, on their original terms. It also forces federal agencies to finish environmental review of any mine plan in the forest within 18 months, and it says the reissued leases cannot be challenged in court. The House passed it along party lines in April 2024; the Senate referred it to committee and never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiary is the company holding the canceled leases, Twin Metals Minnesota, which is owned by the Chilean mining firm Antofagasta and wants to build a large underground copper-nickel mine in the watershed. Supporters, led by Rep. Pete Stauber of northeastern Minnesota, argued the bill would restore mining jobs and tax revenue on the Iron Range, where copper-nickel deposits are among the largest in the world.
analysis.who_benefits_short: A copper mining company and mine jobs

how_it_helps.text: The bill rescinds Public Land Order 7917, the 2023 federal order that withdrew specified Forest Service lands in Cook, Lake, and St. Louis Counties from mineral entry, reopening them to mining claims.

It orders the Interior Department to reissue every mineral lease, preference right lease, and prospecting permit canceled between January 31, 2021 and enactment, on the same terms as before cancellation — restoring the Twin Metals leases the government canceled in 2022.
It bars any court challenge to the reissued leases, removing the main tool opponents have used to slow the project.

It requires the government to finish all environmental and regulatory review of mine plans of operations in the Superior National Forest within 18 months of submission, a faster clock than typical mine permitting.
Supporters argued the region holds one of the world's largest untapped copper-nickel deposits and that mining would bring jobs and tax base to northeastern Minnesota communities.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had become law, the cost would fall on the public and on the local outdoor economy: the Boundary Waters watershed faces the risk of acid mine drainage from sulfide-ore copper mining, pollution that can persist for centuries and is effectively impossible to clean up; outfitters, guides, and lodges that depend on an unspoiled wilderness would bear the economic risk; and taxpayers could be left with cleanup costs if a mine operator failed. Stripping judicial review means citizens could not contest the reissued leases in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Boundary Waters visitors, outfitters, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Sulfide-ore copper mining produces acid mine drainage that can contaminate water for centuries; the bill would open the watershed that drains directly into the Boundary Waters, the most visited wilderness area in the United States, to that risk.
The bill strips judicial review from the reissued leases, so citizens and affected businesses would have no day in court over leases handed back on pre-cancellation terms.

The 18-month deadline for all environmental review compresses the National Environmental Policy Act process for mine plans, reducing the time agencies and the public have to study contamination pathways in a water-rich environment.
The reissued leases return on the same terms as leases originally signed decades ago, locking in terms set before modern environmental analysis of the project.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — potential mining jobs and royalties on a large mineral deposit — is real but speculative, since the bill guarantees only faster permitting, not that a mine would be built or operated safely. The downside is potentially permanent: acid drainage from sulfide mining in the headwaters of the Boundary Waters cannot be reversed, and the bill removes both the buffer (the withdrawal) and the check (judicial review) at the same time. For most people outside the immediate mining districts, the costs outweigh the jobs, which is why environmental groups and the region's recreation economy opposed it and the Senate let it die.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 212-203 on April 30, 2024, the Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee on May 1, and it never got a vote before that Congress ended in January 2025, so the mining ban and the lease cancellations stayed in place.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 10, 2023 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which ordered it reported by a 21-17 committee vote on May 17, 2023.
The committee formally reported the bill on February 9, 2024 and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
On April 29, 2024 the Rules Committee brought the bill to the floor under a closed rule as part of a package of energy and public lands bills.

Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota, whose district includes part of the affected area, moved to recommit the bill — a final attempt to send it back to committee — and the motion failed 205-210, with all 205 voting Democrats in favor and all 210 voting Republicans against.
On final passage the House approved the bill 212-203: Republicans voted 210-0 in favor and Democrats voted 2-203 against.
The Senate received the bill on May 1, 2024 and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where no action followed for the rest of the 118th Congress.
Because the bill never became law, Public Land Order 7917 remained in effect and the canceled mineral leases were not reinstated.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Boundary Waters watershed and the outdoor economy built around it came out ahead: the 20-year federal mining withdrawal remains in force and the Twin Metals leases stay canceled. Mining supporters on the Iron Range gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Boundary Waters and its recreation economy

for.name: Pete Stauber
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee and floor passage.

for.name: 210 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for final passage, 210-0, after all voting Republicans defeated the motion to recommit.

against.name: Betty McCollum
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee on the House floor, a motion that failed 205-210.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 1, 2024 and never voted on it or reported it during the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: on final passage Republicans voted 210-0 yes and Democrats 2-203 no, and the motion to recommit split 205-210 the other way, with every voting Democrat for it and every voting Republican against.

industries.note: The bill would have restored this company's canceled leases on their original terms, forced a fast-tracked 18-month environmental review, and shielded the leases from court challenge — the exact package a single foreign-owned project needed to advance. Its gain runs against the public interest in keeping the Boundary Waters watershed unpolluted, and against the local recreation economy that depends on it.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and tourism around the Boundary Waters (outfitters, guides, lodges)
industries.note: A mine in the watershed would put the clean water the region's outfitting and tourism businesses sell at risk of acid drainage that cannot be cleaned up. These businesses lose under the bill, alongside the visitors and taxpayers who bear the same risk.

The bill creates a template for Congress to rescind land withdrawals by statute, force reissuance of canceled leases, and exempt them from judicial review — precedents that weaken the main public safeguards against mining on federal land nationwide.
